Risk Management ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:02 Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? November 19, 2026 Image On Dec. 18, Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters, and millions of us will happily pay to watch Earth's mightiest heroes face a villain bent on bringing the world to its knees. It's a great escape, partly because we know the heroes always show up in time. Real life offers no such guarantee, and last week showed how close we already live to our own doomsday script. Consider how recently the world ran on paper. Not long ago, people received a printed paycheck every week. Many of us remember our parents planning lunch hours around getting to the bank, or racing there Saturday morning before the branch closed at noon. Bills were paid by paper check, mailed to the mortgage company, the electric company and the oil company. Insuring a car or a house meant calling an agent. Buying anything "from a computer" was pure Isaac Asimov. Today, the entirety of human knowledge fits in a device the size of a deck of cards that nearly everyone carries in their pocket. That has been liberating. But it has also left us almost completely dependent on invisible systems we assume will always be on and safe from disruption, whether the threat is a malfunction, a cyberattack or simple human error. The past week showed how quickly those systems can grind to a halt. On Nov. 12, a Microsoft outage took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot – the backbone of millions of businesses – across dozens of countries for more than half a day. The next afternoon, a communications failure forced the FAA to ground every departing U.S. flight for more than four hours, the longest nationwide shutdown since 9/11. Then on Nov. 16, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase's own hardware disrupted online banking, branch transactions and Zelle payments, spilling over to customers at other banks doing business with Chase. Chase said there was no evidence the outage was cyber-related, and that is exactly the point. If an internal glitch can rattle America's biggest commercial bank, imagine what a deliberate, coordinated attack on power grids, water systems and communications networks could do. Governments urge households to keep emergency supplies, including cash, on hand. Is your company following the same advice? Do business continuity plans cover this? For many companies, the honest answer is "not really." Most plans are built for hurricanes, fires, the loss of a building and other localized events. Backups reside in another state, employees work from home, and operations shift to a recovery site. All of this assumes the Internet, the power grid, and the rest of the economy are still working somewhere . Financial regulators have pushed for more. In 2019, the FFIEC reframed its guidance from business continuity planning to business continuity management, with a focus on operational resilience and the ripple effects of outages across the financial system. The industry also created Sheltered Harbor , a standard for backing up critical customer account data nightly to an offline, air-gapped vault so customers can still reach their funds after a worst-case cyber event. Sheltered Harbor is now winding down, with its specification moving to its parent, FS-ISAC, but the principle stands. Still, even these measures assume someone, somewhere, can restore the data and run the systems. A nationwide, prolonged outage is a scenario few plans address head-on. Can companies function when the rest of the world can't? Not entirely. If customers can't reach essential services, payment rails are down and vendors go dark, no amount of preparation will preserve business as usual. But "not entirely" is materially different from "not at all." The goal is keeping your promises: knowing who your customers are, what they own and what you owe them, and honoring the most critical obligations through manual processes until systems return. That is what makes recovery possible, and it preserves trust when it matters most. Building on the plan you already have Organizations don't need to start over. They need to extend the plans they already have: Add a "dark scenario." Model a weeklong nationwide Internet and communications outage combined with an attack that corrupts your own backups. Ask what breaks first. Define minimum viable operations. For an insurer, that may mean confirming coverage, taking claims, and issuing emergency payments for catastrophic losses. For a bank, it may be cash access, balance verification, and critical payments. Everything else can wait. Keep offline, immutable copies of critical data. Maintain air-gapped backups, plus periodic printed records of policies, account balances, and key contacts. Bring back the manual playbook. Stock paper claim forms and check stock, set pre-approved emergency payment limits and clear signatory authority, and keep the procedures in print. Give a defined role to people with institutional memory of how the work got done before your digital transformation. Plan communications without the Internet. Think satellite phones, two-way radios, pre-arranged meeting points, and agreements with local broadcasters to reach customers. Pressure-test your vendors. Your plan is only as strong as your cloud providers, core processors and payment networks. Know what each would do in this scenario. Take care of your people. Employees will face the same disruption at home. Plan for staff who can't get to work, need cash, or must care for their families. Practice it. Run tabletop exercises in which nothing digital works. Gaps found in a conference room cost far less than gaps found in a crisis. Will you really be there? Nearly every bank and insurance ad promises some version of "we're there when you need us." Those promises were written with storms, fires, and floods in mind. But a slogan has no fine print. When the screens go dark, customers will expect the companies that made those promises to show up. Insurers, whose very reason for being is to anticipate the worst, are well placed to lead, both by hardening their own operations and by helping clients understand how their coverage would respond to a systemic event. Would a cyber or business interruption policy respond to a days-long cloud outage that wasn't caused by an attack? To a bank glitch that delays payroll? After last week, many risk managers are likely asking those questions for the first time. Insurers and brokers with clear answers ready will earn trust before the next outage arrives. In the end, a policy or a bank account is a promise, and trust is what customers are really buying. A company that goes silent in a crisis may never regain it. One that shows up, even with a pen, a paper form, and a phone tree, will be remembered for it. Is it really possible to be fully prepared? No organization can solve everything a large-scale shutdown would throw at it. But there is a big difference between a plan that misses a few angles and one undone by what the 9/11 Commission called a "failure of imagination." The organizations that have thought it through, protected their data, and kept manual workflows open will be the ones that help their customers first and recover fastest. In the movies, doomsday is averted by heroes in capes. In real life, it will be survived thanks to the continuity planner with a binder of printed procedures, the claims veteran who remembers how to cut a paper check, and the IT lead who already knows which vendor to call. They are the real superheroes. Now is the time to give them what they need. Households once ran on a checkbook, a stamp, and a Saturday trip to the bank. Could your company run that way again if it had to? Diane Brassard James Ballot

why_it_matters.en: For insurers and risk professionals, these events underscore the necessity of revising business continuity plans to account for systemic risks and ensure the ability to meet obligations during widespread disruptions. This is crucial for maintaining trust and operational viability in the face of potential catastrophic events.

why_it_matters.fr: Cette évolution peut modifier les exigences de reporting, de capital ou de gouvernance. Les actuaires doivent vérifier les impacts sur les hypothèses, les contrôles et les livrables réglementaires.

items.actuarial_angle: 可能改变核保、定价、理赔、反欺诈、客户运营和模型治理方式。
actions: 判断技术处于概念验证、试点、规模化还是监管约束阶段。

检查模型风险：公平性、可解释性、漂移监控、人工复核和数据授权。

items.title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.original_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_title: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline
items.rss_description: AI Threatens Career Development Pipeline Talent Gap ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:05 As AI automates entry-level insurance tasks, insurance industry leaders must design experiences to develop professional judgment in emerging talent. November 19, 2026 Image Back in the '90s, I was a beast at reconciling spreadsheets. The 10 fingers I'm using to type these lines used to set my "10-key" numeric keypad ablaze. But if you're among the younger readers to come across this article, you'll have no idea what I'm talking about. And as a society, I think that's for the best. A core promise of technological advancement is to eliminate drudgery, like using a 10-key to enter vast amounts of numeric data. In property and casualty insurance, we have spent decades trying to remove mundane work from the lives of underwriters, claims professionals, and technologists. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. But amid the terrific change lurks an industry-scale problem. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? That replacement system needs a name and, more importantly, an owner. Architecting Experience is the framework of deliberately designed exposures, decisions, and feedback loops through which people develop professional judgment and decision context. Cracks in the career ladder Stanford's Digital Economy Lab analyzed payroll data on millions of U.S. jobs through June 2026 and found no economy-wide displacement from AI. What they did find was new employment among 22- to 25-year-olds lagging in industries heavily affected by AI, by about 19% compared to less-affected industries.[1] The employment ladder isn't broken, but some rungs at the bottom are disappearing, which makes it a whole lot harder to climb. Even where junior positions aren't disappearing, the formative skills they help develop are the easiest to automate. In insurance, applied experience and apprenticeship have built the tacit knowledge and judgment needed for success for generations. After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. But when this repetitive and seemingly menial work is delegated to AI, younger staff are deprived of the very task-level experiences they need to develop the business EQ, empathy, and scar tissue that will someday make them senior. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. In their 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, PwC looked at over a billion job advertisements. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. PwC described the trend as the "seniorization" of junior work.[2] A short-term view of AI-driven task optimization will only make the problem worse. For senior employees, more demanding tasks feel more meaningful and engaging than rote work. But the type of work that is most interesting to a seasoned professional isn't necessarily the type of work best suited to creating one. And meaningful work sounds wonderful until every task is a demanding one, and the much-needed Easy Tuesday becomes as much of a relic as my most trusty 10-digit keypad. Clear the slop from the stream BCG recently surveyed 11,749 workers across 14 markets about their use of AI at work. Two-thirds of regular AI users reported increased job satisfaction. At the same time, 41% reported increased mental strain. Half said they were spending more time managing and directing AI than doing the underlying work itself.[3] "Brain fry" refers to the mental fatigue associated with information overload from increased AI oversight.[4] With AI, any junior underwriter can generate a 40-page report with the aplomb of a managing director. But then, the report has to be checked. Preferably by someone with enough know-how to identify and correct mistakes. Without guardrails, we quickly end up in a system where our young talent can access AI-powered tools that allow them to produce work that looks good, but is actually riddled with problems. These problems are then sent upstream to more senior resources who have to spend their time fixing this "workslop"[5]. Junior professionals learn nothing in the process, and increase the workload of their most knowledgeable, and often most expensive, colleagues. When we claim AI is changing the way we work, we're giving the tool too much credit, while absolving ourselves of responsibility. The truth is, AI isn't changing the way we work. Our decision-makers are. And if, as a result of these changes and the adoption of AI, the leaders break the career ladder, they are responsible for engineering a new one. AI-resilient architecture I'm not in favor of clinging to rote work out of nostalgia. AI very much has a place in our workflows, and I remain bullish on the beneficial role of AI over the long term. But today, as we are all still sorting out the impacts and influences of AI on real people, we must think things through holistically and humanistically from the very beginning. In the face of AI removing traditional and lower-level tasks, the implications of this must be assessed, and solutions for the resultant gaps must be created. When architecting experience for new talent, what matters is to look at tasks through the dual lens of raw efficiency and professional development. Do the tasks teach the rules of the game, and more importantly, when the rules stop applying? Do they offer a chance to shadow a more seasoned professional to develop situational awareness and understanding of context? Do they help build judgment? Do they create the kinds of relationships every business is built on? These answers will help inform which tasks to automate, and which need more thought. A "yes" doesn't mean the task cannot be handed off to automation; it means the developmental value has to be preserved, somehow. The oversight role for management is to understand and enforce the right order of operations: organic brain first, neural network second. As with all complex systems, architecting experience isn't a blueprint. It's a process bound to yield different results for different organizations. Once the initial assessment is complete, ideally under the supervision of an executive with accountability, the hard work of execution, review, and adaptation begins. The good news is: there's plenty of responsibility to go around. Executive management must identify the experiences that create expertise, design a plan for succession, and own how the business will look ten years down the road. Elsewhere, HR and development teams have a responsibility to engineer the learning experiences and coaching or apprenticeship infrastructure, while managers can iterate, suggest improvements, and raise the red flag when skills aren't being developed. Tech and risk teams also have a clear role to observe AI usage, monitor costs and defect rates, and flag when automated work misses the mark. Senior professionals must keep in mind that juniors need engagement, context, and good professional models to follow, while the juniors themselves must remember to think first and ask AI second. Insurance is still early in the AI adoption process, and fortunate to have a deep bench of experienced professionals around the world, alongside ambitious newcomers. But every day, AI offers new deployment opportunities for efficiency and optimization. The greatest organizations of tomorrow will not only be able to harness those opportunities, but will also succeed in architecting experience for the next generation of world-class talent. We made great strides with Robotic Process Automation (RPA), leaps with broader Intelligent Automation (IA), and now a phenomenal bound with Artificial Intelligence (AI), which promises to revolutionize the way we work. While our job definitions and related skills are morphing at an absurdly fast rate, how do we ensure that emerging talent has the opportunity to develop the depth of understanding and judgment their predecessors possess, even while AI is tending to disassociate humans from some of the traditional activities of their craft? After ingesting enough submissions, you develop a second sense for when a detail looks off, or when risks that look identical stem from entirely different causes. What our young talent are left with are the tasks too difficult for AI, and sometimes beyond the judgment they possess. They found that heavily AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to demand senior capabilities—like judgment, leadership, and interpersonal skills—than the jobs least exposed to AI. items.title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.original_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_title: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start
items.rss_description: Why New Producers Stall Before They Start Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Tue, 11/17/2026 - 15:15 Four-year producer retention has sat near 14% for years. One overlooked cause: new producers are handed materials that promote the company but give prospects no reason to trust the person. November 19, 2026 Image Even with aptitude and personality testing, only about 14% of new financial professionals have still been under contract four years after they were hired, according to LIMRA. The losses come early. First-year retention runs from 44% to 55%, depending on who recruited the producer. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. I've come to believe we're overlooking one piece of the problem: the gap between marketing and sales. Marketing departments produce great materials that promote the brand and its products. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. Conventional e-newsletters contribute to inbox glut Most new producers are sent out with the same tools as everyone else: a business card, perhaps a company newsletter, and a set of pre-approved PDFs. The newsletter is the piece most firms count on to keep prospects warm, and it has five weaknesses. They are too long. Attention spans are short, and screen after screen asks for more time than most readers will give. They make readers scroll to choose. Readers scroll down to see what's there, then back up to decide. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. They lack creative calls to action or lead magnets of value. Readers see a "Subscribe" or "Get my 5 tips" button as permission to receive spam. They speak for the company, not the person. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. A better newsletter respects the reader's time: one page with links to no more than three pieces of content. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. What a first impression could be Social media posts, newsletters, mail, and product information all have their place in the sales cycle, but on their own, none of them builds a relationship. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. In large organizations, lead gates usually sit on the company website, not on individual producers' pages, so the contact information goes to the company or agency. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. Put together, these elements give a new producer something memorable that builds trust: a personal profile, an approved multimedia brochure, and a way to find the people worth calling. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. It requires looking at a new producer's first 90 days from the prospect's side of the table. Audit the first impression. Gather everything a new producer can send a prospect in week one. Then ask: Why would I choose this producer over another? Put the person up front. Give each new producer a short video or audio introduction about who they are, not what they do. All your producers do similar work. Who they are is what sets them apart. Cover every format. Pair each key message with something to read, something to watch or hear, and something to try. In a newsletter, that means no more than three pieces, each labeled with its format and length. Host it; don't attach it. Sharing content by link keeps the company in control and ensures only approved, up-to-date materials circulate. Watch the early signals. Lack of activity is an early warning sign, and analytics can now measure it. Managers can see which channels drive activity and which new recruits may need help sooner. Have it ready before the first appointment. A fast start depends on what the producer can share in the first week, not the first quarter. Give them something worth answering Pushing prospects with a stick instead of offering a carrot gives the industry a black eye. The better path is to make sure that when prospects look, they find a real person, in a format they can take in, with content that compliance approved and still under control. The four-year retention number has held steady for a long time. Leaders have told us that early activity matters. When a new producer leaves within two years, the recruiting effort, the licensing, the training, and the manager's time are lost. The industry has refined selection, adjusted financing plans, and built mentoring programs. Yet the four-year number has barely moved. I spent more than 25 years in this industry as a producer, a wholesaler, and a group long-term care presenter. But those materials don't help producers distinguish themselves from colleagues who hand out the same materials. The most successful practices are built on trust. A prospect won't discuss their financial or insurance problems until they trust the producer enough to reveal highly personal information. Insurance companies have a reputation for being conservative and not on the leading edge of new technology. Perhaps it's in our DNA as managers of risk. There has always been a tension between what we can do and what we're allowed to do: a tug of war between sales and compliance. What leaders say keeps producers In a 2022 study, LIMRA and Finseca asked field and home-office leaders which factors do the most to keep new producers past year two. They named five: early activity (a fast start), a strong selection process before hiring, joint field work, quality sales skills training, and mentoring. Field leaders also listed lack of early activity among the causes of termination. Four of those five factors are about the producer: who we hire and how we train and support them. Early activity is different. It depends on two people: the producer must reach out, and the prospect has to respond. Prospects respond to people they feel a connection with. What constitutes activity? When I began, it meant 10 meetings a week with new prospects, all of them in person. You left behind a business card and a generic company brochure and hoped you'd made enough of an impression to earn a second appointment. Today, a new producer may reach out in person or virtually. Either way, the takeaway must be memorable. A business card or marketing piece that provides an experience rather than just data can raise a producer's MQ (memorability quotient) significantly. The format gap Producers are largely on their own in building trust, and the materials they're handed don't help much. The World Life Insurance Report 2027, published in September 2026 by Capgemini and LIMRA, surveyed 6,175 consumers in 18 countries. More than 40% of those considering coverage felt confused, uncertain, or unconvinced by what they found, and one in four dropped out before buying. Overly technical language was the top reason, cited by 37%. Eighty-five percent of those consumers want to interact with an advisor at some point, and two-thirds prefer a human advisor when they finalize coverage. The demand for the producer is there. The materials can get in the way instead of advancing the relationship. Research shows what helps. In an experiment by the Society of Actuaries Research Institute and RGA, summaries, FAQs, and simple icons raised comprehension by 21%. Interactive elements, such as a needs calculator, raised it by 28%. On a page that used both, adding video raised it another 15%. Imagine delivering all that through something as simple as a business card. People, both prospects and producers, differ in many ways. Finding commonality is key to establishing a relationship. Half of consumers in the Capgemini–LIMRA study said they prefer advisors with similar demographic characteristics. And in the SOA–RGA experiment, comprehension rose significantly when participants saw the presenter as credible, expert, and from a similar cultural background. As a long-term care insurance wholesaler, I often funded advisors' client events: dinners meant to turn prospects into clients. Most guests didn't know the advisor or had only a passing acquaintance with him. At one event I sponsored, the advisor spent little time presenting himself and concentrated on the features and benefits of the coverage from the company I represented. He didn't convert a single prospect, and I got zero return on my investment. The guests had no reason to trust the person in front of them, so the product never had a chance. We can't know in advance who is on the other end of a producer's outreach. Some prospects read. Some watch. Some listen. Some need to try a calculator before they believe anything. The safest approach is to offer something for each of them, with the producer's own face and voice up front. They are too long. Many give up first. They are mostly text. Email can carry video and interactive tools, but few firms use them. Prospects who would rather watch or listen find little to engage them. Prospects learn about the carrier's strength and products, but nothing about the producer who sent it. There is also a compliance cost. Approved PDFs get downloaded, forwarded, and kept long after they've been revised. A PDF attached in March can still be circulating in October, carrying last spring's disclosure. Meanwhile, new producers who need to be noticed improvise with homemade posts and flyers. Producers need to be seen, and compliance needs control. At a glance, the reader sees each title, whether it's an article, a video, or a podcast, and about how long it will take. They choose in seconds, without scrolling, in the format they prefer. And because the pieces are links, not downloads, compliance retains more control. Today's technology can ease the tension between sales and compliance. Personal profiles with video and text, built on a company-approved template, let every producer present themselves authentically by email, on social media and websites, and through "phygital" marketing: digital content delivered through physical objects such as business cards, printed materials, or promotional merchandise. An agency or firm can start with business cards, where a scan or a tap opens a short personal video scripted to feature the "who" and not the "what" along with their bio, contact information, and compliance-approved content. Data alone isn't memorable. Experiences are. The company brochure can travel the same way. Printed brochures are costly and usually end up in the circular file. The same approved piece can live behind the producer's card instead, with no reprint charges, unlimited distribution, and home-office updates that take effect everywhere at once. Stories engage far better than statistics. Say a new producer targets young couples buying their first home who need to protect their mortgage. They need life insurance, and so do growing families and pre-retirees who want to transfer wealth efficiently. A firm could offer a choice of short, approved videos, each speaking to a different audience, that drop into the same approved brochure that explains different types of life insurance. Then add a lead gate, a short form that asks for a prospect's contact details in exchange for content of value. Placed in the producer's own piece, a lead gate helps a new producer build a prospect list from the first week. No study yet measures the effect directly, but the evidence points the same way. What leaders can do now None of this requires a new distribution model. items.title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps

items.rss_title: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps
items.rss_description: $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Exposes Insurance Gaps Cyber ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/18/2026 - 14:34 The $6.3 billion Binance theft bypassed private keys entirely, exposing gaps in how crypto risks are underwritten and covered. November 19, 2026 Image On Oct. 29, attackers took roughly $6.3 billion out of Binance's hot wallets in about 20 minutes. It is the largest crypto theft on record, and the FBI has tied it to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance has since committed to absorbing the financial impact of the incident. By Oct. 31, it reported that 98% of the affected token assets had been replenished. How it happened matters more than how much According to Binance's incident report, the campaign ran for months. One engineer installed a tampered developer tool in June. Another was compromised in September through a fake coding assignment. In October, the attackers used an internal AI tool to get into more machines and finally took control of the system that approves wallet transactions. The key detail for insurance: Binance says no private keys were stolen. The attackers didn't need them. They controlled the system that signs transactions, so it signed whatever the attackers asked. Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Ben Slagis

Underwriting conversations with crypto clients have long centered on keys. Where are they stored? Who holds them? How many people have to sign off? This loss shows that everything around the keys (people, laptops, software and approval systems) matters just as much. What this means for the insurance market Tougher questions. Crime and specie applications will dig into employee devices, developer tools, and internal AI tools. Underwriters will want to know who can push code into live systems and how fast a wallet can be frozen once something looks wrong. More caution on hot wallets. Offline cold storage has always been easier to insure than online hot wallets used for everyday withdrawals. After watching billions leave hot wallets in minutes, insurers will be more careful about how much limit they put there and what they charge. More disputes over which policy pays. Crypto losses tend to fall between cyber and crime policies, and this attack sits right on the line. Cyber or crime? Four common mix-ups "We have cyber, so a hack is covered." Cyber pays for the cleanup - forensics, legal advice, customer notices, data lawsuits, and lost income while systems are down. Most cyber policies exclude the theft or transfer of funds, and many exclude digital assets. Cyber may pay for the investigation but not the stolen assets. "We have crime, so theft is covered." A standard crime policy protects money, securities and other property. Without an endorsement, crypto may not clearly fit. Specie policies often cover cold storage only, with hot wallets excluded or sublimited. "Computer fraud and funds transfer fraud are the same thing." They aren't. Computer fraud usually needs a hacker to change data or force a transfer. Funds transfer fraud usually involves fake instructions sent to a bank. An exchange signing its own blockchain transaction may not fit neatly into either. "Our people were tricked, so social engineering coverage applies." Expect a debate. Social engineering coverage usually responds when an employee is fooled into sending money, often with a small sublimit. Here, engineers were tricked into installing bad software, not sending funds. What brokers should review before the next renewal Map the gaps. Lay the crime, specie, cyber, tech E&O, and D&O policies side by side and walk through this scenario. Who pays for the stolen assets, the forensics, and the lawsuits? Check the "other insurance" clauses, since cyber and crime policies sometimes each point to the other. Compare limits to real exposure. Ask how much the client keeps in hot wallets on a normal day and a busy day, then compare that to the limit they're buying. Talk about the reserve fund. Many exchanges keep their own fund to repay customers. That isn't insurance, and if it's held in crypto, its value can drop right when it's needed. Don't forget D&O. Lawsuits and regulators usually follow a large loss, often in more than one country. Directors and officers will want to know their coverage holds up. Looking ahead There is some good news here. About $2.85 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen or intercepted, mostly stablecoins whose issuers can block them, and Binance has said customers will be covered. Insurance capacity for digital asset companies keeps growing. More insurers are willing to write crime, specie and D&O for crypto businesses than a few years ago, and one event shouldn't reverse that. But more capacity doesn't mean easier terms. This single loss accounts for nearly three-quarters of the crypto hacking losses recorded this year. Headline events like this make underwriters more careful. Expect longer applications, more underwriting meetings and a closer look at how controls work day to day. Vague answers will cost you. For brokers, the job is easy to describe and hard to do. Understand how the client actually operates, not just where the keys are kept, and make sure the coverage matches. The clients who can show their work will get the best of the new capacity. The next renewal is the right time to start that conversation. Get Involved Our authors are what set Insurance Thought Leadership apart. items.title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.original_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_title: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent
items.rss_description: When Customers Get Their Own Chatbot Agent PaulCarroll Sun, 11/22/2026 - 21:48 For some years now, I've been developing what I call the Laws of Zero. The notion is that the price of certain digital goods looks like it's headed toward zero if you map the cost curve out five or 10 years -- computing power, communication, sensors and cameras, in particular, have all seen exponential declines. So you should plan as though you will have an infinite supply of those goods. Thinking about zero cost has been a useful exercise for businesses... but AI is now driving the cost of intelligence toward zero, too, which will provide what feel like infinite amounts of it to customers. They're going to use it. We've already seen how AI has changed online search and started to alter many shopping behaviors. But AI agents will also mean that there will be essentially zero marginal cost for customers who want to request an update on an insurance claim, who want to complain, who want to challenge a bill, or who want any other sort of service. Meta's recent announcement of its Muse personal agent is just the start. The floodgates are about to open. Let's have a look. The positive response to Meta's announcement shows that the clock has started ticking on the trend toward vastly more customer service contacts. There will be the usual sorts of growing pains as the technology is being adopted -- there have already been reports of the AI agent getting into user data, such as bank records, that were supposed to be off limits -- so you won't be inundated right away. But the change is coming, so you might as well start planning. Think about all the calls you don't make and emails you don't send about a product or service you've bought because you don't have the time or just don't want to deal with the hassle. Lots of companies make considerable profit off the fact that people don't get around to canceling subscriptions. Then imagine what happens when someone can just tell an agent to make that contact -- or when the agent simply does the work on its own because it knows you want it to. That ease of contact issue hit home for me a couple of months ago, when my older daughter wrote an article for the Travel section of the Wall Street Journal. In my 17 years at the WSJ, the most letters I got on an article was maybe 300, and my daughter beat that on her first try. There were close to 300 comments on the article, and she received maybe 200 emails routed through the WSJ. The reason -- other than the fact that she wrote a great piece -- was that readers back in the 1990s had to type out a letter, surely in a formal style, use White-Out to fix any errors, find the right address in the paper's masthead, address the envelope, put a stamp on it and mail it. With my daughter, an online reader just had to hit the "comment" button or the "email" button and start typing. Ease of access will cause the same sort of increase in contacts for insurance companies. Meta even used a question about an insurance bill as an example of what Muse Wonder can do in an initial promotional video. (The example begins at the 2:27 mark here .) A couple of initial thoughts on how to get ready: For starters, you want to do everything you can to reduce the need for customers to wonder about anything. Amazon, in its early days, treated every contact by a customer as signifying a failure, and you should adopt that same mindset. I realize that will be far harder in insurance, with its complex processes and contracts, than it is in book selling. Still, every question that doesn't arise is one you don't have to figure out how to answer. Every update you provide is one the customer or their AI agent doesn't have to request. You'll also want to think about how to make your systems as accessible as possible to AI -- within privacy restrictions, regulation, etc. That effort will include sorting out which queries are from an AI, so you can have your AI deal with the customers' agents as much as possible and only bring in your human staff when necessary. The sooner you get started planning for the onslaught of customer inquiries, the better prepared you'll be. Zero is a magic number. Free is an unbeatable cost. Cheers, Paul P.S. If you're intrigued by my favorite topic, the Laws of Zero, the most complete explanation I've developed is in a book I wrote with Chunka Mui and Tim Andrews, " A Brief History of a Perfect Future: Inventing the World We Can Proudly Leave Our Kids by 2050 ." Image Paul Carroll While the focus to this point has been on customers potentially using AI agents to shop for insurance, people will also use them to demand much more service. Much more. items.rss_title: Microsoft Declares ‘Code Red’ After Historic Outage, Internal Memos Show

items.extracted_text: Microsoft Declares ‘Code Red’ After Historic Outage, Internal Memos Show Article 0 Comments Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. The November 12-13 outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms and disrupted airline communications, fueling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents. Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption. The Code Red signified the most severe and urgent alert to address weaknesses in Microsoft’s engineering and operational practices after the outage disrupted Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 products. It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added. ‘Fog of War’ Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company’s workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo. “Our work doesn’t end when service is restored. Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority,” a company spokesperson told Reuters when contacted about the memos. Recovery Target As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions. Slow Patch Deployments “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said “urgent patches to our M365 Core services” took too long to deploy worldwide. “In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” he wrote. items.title: Construction-Defect Lawsuit Clock Starts at Occupancy, NC Appeals Court Says
items.original_title: Construction-Defect Lawsuit Clock Starts at Occupancy, NC Appeals Court Says
items.rss_title: Construction-Defect Lawsuit Clock Starts at Occupancy, NC Appeals Court Says
items.rss_description: Insurers hoping to sue contractors in subrogation over construction defects are strictly bound by North Carolina’s six-year statute of repose—which starts at occupancy, even if some repairs were made years after a structure was completed, the state’s Court of Appeals …
items.extracted_text: Construction-Defect Lawsuit Clock Starts at Occupancy, NC Appeals Court Says Article 0 Comments Insurers hoping to sue contractors in subrogation over construction defects are strictly bound by North Carolina’s six-year statute of repose—which starts at occupancy, even if some repairs were made years after a structure was completed, the state’s Court of Appeals said last week. “Allowing the statute of repose to toll or start running anew each time a repair is made would subject a defendant to potential open-ended liability for an indefinite period of time, defeating the very purpose of statutes of repose,” the appeals court wrote in Holton vs. Valuebuild Homes et al , quoting from 1999 and 2014 appellate court decisions. The court explained that Nate and Christine Holton in 2015 contracted with Value Build Homes for construction of a residence in Moore County. A certificate of occupancy was issued on May 17, 2016. Within weeks, though, part of the kitchen floor began sagging. The contractor’s workers came and stabilized the area. Later, the plaintiff homeowners said the house was never level and had presented defects since they had moved in. In 2023, after consulting another contractor, the couple told the homebuilder that they were concerned that the house had been built on an improperly sloped ground or foundation. Value Build Homes workers looked at the property in 2024 and took some measurements, the court opinion explained. It wasn’t until January 2025, more than eight years after the clock on the North Carolina statute of repose had started running, that the homeowners filed suit against the homebuilder, alleging breach of contract, construction defects, and negligence. A trial court judge agreed with the defendant homebuilder and granted summary judgment, effectively dismissing the lawsuit. The Holtons appealed, arguing that the 2024 visit by the builder should have restarted the statute of repose clock, allowing the lawsuit to continue. North Carolina’s repose statute reads: ” …a plaintiff has the burden of showing that he or she brought the action within six years of either (1) the substantial completion of the house or (2) the specific last act or omission of defendant giving rise to the cause of action.” But the Court of Appeals, in the opinion written by Judge Allegra Collins, emphasized the first part of that law. Previous court rulings have held that a building is substantially complete when certificate of occupancy is issued. A simple repair does not qualify as a “last act” under the statute, the opinion found, citing other court decisions. The evidence “shows that defendants investigated plaintiffs’ complaints in 2024 by excavating near the foundation and taking measurements. Investigative activities of this nature do not constitute construction work or repairs extending the statutory repose period,” Judge Collins wrote. And because the plaintiffs had stated that “the house was never level since day 1,” that showed that the homeowners knew early on about the problem and could have sued before the six-year window closed. “Unlike a wholly latent condition, the condition forming the basis of plaintiffs’ claims was apparent in 2016,” the court said. Likewise, the homeowners’ lawsuit was barred by statutes of limitations, which carry four and three-year clocks. And because the owners and the builder’s relationship is governed by contract, purely economic losses are not recoverable under North Carolina statute and case law. “The undisputed forecast of evidence demonstrates that Plaintiffs became aware of the condition underlying their claims in 2016 but waited until 2025 to file suit,” the court concluded. “Their claims are therefore barred by statute of repose and, independently, by the applicable statutes of limitation. Plaintiffs’ negligence claim is barred by the economic loss rule, and Plaintiffs failed to forecast evidence sufficient to support a claim for unfair and deceptive trade practices. We thus affirm the trial court’s summary judgment order.” North Carolina’s six-year statute of repose is shorter than some states, longer than others. Florida lawmakers, for example, in 2023 shortened the Florida statute to seven years from 10. It, too, starts the clock at the certificate of occupancy. Tennessee has one of the shorter statutes, at four years, the Gordon & Rees law firm has blogged. Some states, including New York and Vermont, do not have a construction-defect statute of repose, SDV Fenchurch law firm noted. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.rss_title: Berkshire-Owned Utility Lauds Oregon High Court’s Expanded Review of Wildfire Suit

items.extracted_text: Berkshire-Owned Utility Lauds Oregon High Court’s Expanded Review of Wildfire Suit Article 0 Comments Berkshire Hathaway’s PacifiCorp utility said on Saturday it welcomed a decision by the Oregon Supreme Court to look into all potential errors in the handling of a wildfire class-action against the company. Oregon residents and business owners who want PacifiCorp to be held liable for four wildfires in 2020 hope to reverse a state appeals court’s decision that wiped out $1.25 billion of awards to 201 plaintiffs because of an error with the instructions to jurors. Related: Berkshire-Owned PacifiCorp Wins Ruling That Could Reduce Oregon Wildfire Damages But the state’s highest court on Friday expanded its review of the case to include all possible errors raised in the appeal, not just the jury instructions. That may increase the possibility that the state Supreme Court will find problems in the trial judge’s handling of the litigation, including whether he should have certified a class to begin with. Friday’s decision means Portland-based PacifiCorp will not face additional so-called mini-trials over its liability to fire victims while the appeals process continues. “The Court recognizes the litany of missteps in this case, and we remain confident that sound legal principles and facts will prevail,” Ryan Flynn, president of PacifiCorp’s Pacific Power division, said in a statement released on Saturday. Attorneys for the plaintiffs did not immediately comment on the order. If plaintiffs win the lawsuit, PacifiCorp could face tens of billions of dollars in potential damages over its role in the 2020 wildfires. More than 2,400 plaintiffs blamed the Portland-based utility’s equipment and alleged negligent failure to shut down power lines during a Labor Day weekend windstorm for damaging more than 2,000 properties. The state’s high court heard oral arguments in the case earlier this month. The appeals court’s decision focused on the jury instruction by Multnomah County Circuit Court Judge Steffan Alexander, and not whether a class action was justified. Friday’s order set deadlines in early 2027 for the parties to file briefs on the broader set of appellate issues. items.extracted_text: ESMA proposal to limit cat bonds in UCITS funds leaves investors with greater risk: Plenum's Grieger - Artemis.bm ESMA proposal to limit cat bonds in UCITS funds leaves investors with greater risk: Plenum’s Grieger 24th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard In a pointed critique of the European Securities and Markets Authority’s (ESMA) push to cap UCITS catastrophe bond allocations at 10%, Daniel Grieger, Managing Partner and Senior Portfolio Manager at Plenum Investments argues that the regulator’s risk assessment relies on isolated loss events while ignoring decades of empirical data and evidence. The Portfolio Manager emphasises that restricting access to an asset class with a fraction of equity market drawdowns and a 0.22 correlation to stocks will leave retail investors more exposed to broader market crashes, not less. Earlier this year, Plenum Investments, the catastrophe bond and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, published a position paper communicating its thoughts on the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) recommendation regarding cat bond eligibility under the UCITS investment framework. In the paper, Plenum Investments shared its opinions on the ESMA recommendation, highlighting that catastrophe bonds are a mature asset class that has been successfully integrated into UCITS over a long period of time. Building on that critique, Grieger takes aim at ESMA’s risk assessment of catastrophe bond funds in its TRV Risk Monitor 1/2026 , with the manager stressing that ESMA draws attention to retail investor risks it considers particularly concerning, while simultaneously pointing to its proposal to restrict the allocation of catastrophe bonds in UCITS funds to 10%. The Portfolio Manager says the assessment of the asset class presented in the TRV Risk Monitor does not stand up to critical scrutiny, neither against ESMA’s own findings, or against the experience of market participants, nor against a sound statistical data analysis. “Particularly irritating is the fact that ESMA highlights the supposedly high risks of CAT Bonds without systematically comparing them with the risks of traditional asset classes. This creates the impression that the tail risk associated with extreme events is a specific feature of CAT Bonds rather than a fundamental phenomenon common to all asset classes,” Grieger commented. Grieger affirms that the rationale rests on two isolated events: the total loss of Jamaica’s $150 million IBRD CAR Jamaica 2024 parametric catastrophe bond from the impacts of last year’s Hurricane Melissa, and the ongoing loss assessments related to the Los Angeles wildfires from early 2025. “It ignores the fact that comparable extreme risks also exist in equity markets – just in a different form and with potentially equally serious consequences. Moreover, the Jamaica bond represents around 0.3% of the market. ESMA provides no figures for the overall market (Swiss Re Cat Bond Index TR) – these would have shown that, since the inception of the CAT Bond market, the maximum loss was -15.3%, compared with -57.1% for equities as measured by the MSCI World Net TR Index. Recovery took 8.5 months in the CAT Bond market and 5.6 years for equities,” Grieger said. The manager also argues that ESMA’s own findings contradicts its own conclusion, highlighting that the organisation has previously stated that catastrophe bonds have so far rarely suffered a total loss, and that the funds have achieved relatively stable returns, usually holding more than 100 positions, show only limited concentration risks and maintain liquidity buffers of 5 to 10%. None of which, according to Grieger implies an increased risk for retail investors. Furthermore, Grieger stresses that equities are permitted without limit in UCITS and can also be purchased directly by retail investors but clarified though that since 2003 they have lost up to -57.1%, were in negative territory in 21.5% of all 12-month periods and fall sharply precisely in times of crisis. “CAT Bonds, by contrast, with a quarter of the maximum loss and a seventh of the negative periods (3.2%), are to be capped at 10%. The same applies to tail risk (VaR 99%, 12 months): for CAT Bonds, the RMS simulation (Moody’s RMS Miu) yields -30.69%, and even this 1-in-100 scenario has never been reached – the worst 12 months came in at -11.1%. For equities, a considerably lower value of -42.5% is not modelled but has actually occurred since 2003,” the manager explains. He continued: “Of all segments, it is precisely the one with the lower extreme risk that is to be capped. A risk-based approach would reach the opposite conclusion. Looking at the risks in the equity market since the late 1980s – the 1987 stock market crash, the first and second Asian crises in the late 1990s, the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, the 2008 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID-19 crisis, the 2022 interest-rate shock and the tariff dispute – the risks appear to be considerably higher than for CAT Bonds.” In addition, independent analyses cover extensive risk metrics for all UCITS cat bond funds, which are required by regulation to publish their holdings twice a year. Yet Grieger also calls out that ESMA has granular portfolio data for only five funds, adding that proposing a cap on this basis that effectively makes pure CAT Bond UCITS impossible is “disproportionate.” Addressing the impact of natural catastrophe events, Grieger points out that catastrophe bonds are designed to adjust continuously. Because they carry short maturities of just a few years, risk models, attachment points, and spreads are regularly repriced to reflect shifting risk assessments. “Since 2003, realised losses have averaged 0.93% p.a., well below the modelled expected loss of 2.3% p.a. The expected loss of the overall market shows a slightly rising trend over the years. This suggests that changing risk conditions, including climate-related influences, are increasingly reflected in modelling and pricing. In addition, ESMA disregards the fact that the CAT Bond market is a so-called top-layer market. This means that CAT Bonds only bear losses once insured losses exceed exceptionally high thresholds. Although an increase in weather-related natural catastrophe losses can be observed, in many cases these do not reach the loss level required to affect the CAT Bond market at all. For earthquake risks, which also account for a substantial share of the CAT Bond market, no climate-change-related change in frequency is to be expected,” Grieger further added. Finally, Grieger also outlines that the cap ultimately increases investors’ risk. “With a correlation of 0.22 to equities and -4.0% during the financial crisis (equities -57.1%), CAT Bonds are among the few investments that provide stability in equity crises. Restricting retail investors’ access deprives them of this diversification instrument and leaves them alone with the greater risk,” he said. In terms of volatility, tail risk, loss frequency, and recovery time, Grieger maintains that catastrophe bonds offer a considerably more favourable risk profile than equities. “Against this background, ESMA’s risk assessment of CAT Bonds in the TRV Risk Monitor No. 1 (2026) warrants critical scrutiny. One would therefore expect ESMA to put the risks it has identified for CAT Bonds in relation to the risks of traditional asset classes. Such a comparative analysis, however, is missing. “Anyone who maintains such unequal treatment despite empirical evidence to the contrary not only jeopardises the credibility and consistency of UCITS regulation, but also raises questions of proportionality and objectivity, especially when investor protection is cited as the central justification,” Grieger explained. items.extracted_text: Howden-backed Novark strengthens Bermuda team with four senior appointments - Artemis.bm Howden-backed Novark strengthens Bermuda team with four senior appointments 24th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Novark Group, the Howden-backed insurance management and securities administration business for insurance-linked securities (ILS) and alternative capital, has appointed four key senior executives within its Bermuda operations. The appointments bring together deep expertise across reinsurance, financial services, capital markets, and technology. Charlotte Brooks is set to take on the role of Head of ILS Compliance and Legal, while Hassan Khan has been appointed Head of ILS Pricing and Analytics. At the same time, Parker Saunders joins the firm as Lead Business Engineer, while Niraj Pritmani also joins as COO of Novark, pending immigration approval. Novark said that all four appointments represent a further investment in Bermuda’s role as a centre for insurance and financial innovation, supporting the development of new structures and solutions as the relationship between insurance risk and institutional capital continues to evolve. Based in Bermuda, Novark Group was launched by Howden Re back in September. The company provides insurance management and securities administration for ILS funds, institutional investors, insurers and reinsurers. Novark also aims to serve as an operational backbone for the ILS and insurance risk asset class, bringing investors, cedants, brokers and administrators together in a single digital environment, giving each of them transparent, near real-time access throughout the lifecycle of transactions and investments. We’ve previously noted that Novark’s launch is a bold move, extending Howden’s services beyond origination, structuring and placement, into the ongoing management and administration of ILS and other alternative capital or structured reinsurance transactions. Just a few months on after its initial launch, Novark is rapidly bolstering its leadership team across Bermuda. Brooks is a qualified UK lawyer and has spent 13 years inhouse at global re/insurance companies advising on multinational transactions. Before she joined Howden Re in 2024, Brooks served as VP Legal Counsel at RenaissanceRe, and also previously served as Associate General Counsel at Validus Re and AIG. In addition, Khan brings more than a decade of expertise in reinsurance pricing, underwriting and risk analytics, across property catastrophe, structured reinsurance and alternative capital. Khan has spent the past 11 years at Allianz Global Corporate & Specialty (AGCS) across London and Hamilton, Bermuda, most recently serving as an Alternative Risk Transfer (ART) Underwriter. He also has a strong track record of leading complex analytical and pricing initiatives, optimising portfolios and turning sophisticated risk analysis into commercial solutions for insurers and reinsurers. Saunders joins the firm with extensive experience in financial technology, software engineering and re/insurance data platforms. As Lead Business Engineer, Saunders will lead the continued development of Novark’s proprietary technology, connecting data, systems and workflows to improve efficiency and the experience of market participants. Lastly, Pritmani joins Novark with over 10 years of experience across alternative capital, insurance and reinsurance, with deep expertise in the Bermuda market. Throughout his career, he has served in various senior leadership roles within the island’s insurance management sector, where he has worked closely with boards, investors and executive teams on strategic initiatives, capital planning, complex transactions and the management of key commercial relationships. Pritmani has also helped establish and oversee many regulated insurance and reinsurance structures throughout his career, as well as help strengthen financial and governance frameworks, and navigate complex insurance and capital markets transactions. Prior to Novark, Pritmani held roles at Artex Risk Solutions, including Client Service Director, Insurance Management and Vice President. He also spent nearly eight years working in financial services audit roles at EY. All four appointments are subject, where applicable, to relevant regulatory approvals, Bermuda immigration and work permit permissions, and completion of employment arrangements. Novark Group also confirmed that Brooks and Khan’s roles will take effect subject to the amendment of their Bermuda work permits. Their responsibilities are subject to established governance, confidentiality and conflict-management arrangements. Razi Naqvi, Director, Novark, commented: “Insurance risk is becoming a core part of institutional portfolios, and investors are right to expect more from the infrastructure behind it. Transparency and strong governance should be a given, not a differentiator. That is the standard Novark has been built to meet.” “What we’ve built is attracting exceptional talent from across sectors – specialists who recognise the opportunity to apply their skills in new ways to support clients and deliver outstanding service. Charlotte, Hassan, Parker and Niraj bring an extraordinary breadth of experience to Novark. Together, we’re combining the institutional standards investors expect with the talent and innovation to help shape the future of this market,” Naqvi continued. Charlotte Brooks, Head of ILS Compliance and Legal, Novark, said: “Bermuda’s position as a leading centre for reinsurance, ILS and institutional insurance capital is built on decades of specialist expertise, sophisticated market infrastructure and a mature, robust and internationally respected regulatory framework. That combination gives investors confidence in the governance, oversight and standards supporting their capital. items.extracted_text: Australia Bolsters Online Safety Law With Tougher Big Tech Fine Article 0 Comments The world’s biggest technology providers may face fines of as much as 5% of their global revenue under Australia’s new Digital Duty of Care law after the government toughened penalties to secure its passage. Communications Minister Anika Wells said Tuesday the bill will pass parliament this week after its amendments won the support of the minority Greens party. The maximum penalty for breaching the law was raised from a previously proposed ceiling of A$109 million ($72 million). The sweeping legislation seeks to reduce online harm by compelling digital service providers from social media platforms to AI chatbots to build safety into their products. It will also allow social media users to switch off algorithms that determine what content they see. Australians would also be able to sue companies for harm caused by breaches of the law. Wells described the legislation as Australia’s most significant step yet to improve online safety. Wells said in an interview last month that she wants to use the legislation as a step toward working with other countries and establish basic online safety standards, particularly for children. items.extracted_text: Next Supplier Hit by Cyberattack in Latest UK Retail Breach Article 0 Comments Next Plc said an online supplier suffered a breach that allowed unauthorized access to certain data relating to the retailer, the latest in a string of U.K. companies to be caught in cyberattacks. The affected information is benign and can’t be used to facilitate fraud against customers or the company, the clothing and homeware retailer said Monday. No customer personal data has been compromised, it said. Next is confident that its own systems haven’t been compromised but said it’s “treating the matter with the utmost seriousness.” The retailer did not identify the supplier or specify what data had been accessed. It said it’s working with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities as it continues to look into the nature and scope of the incident. The disclosure adds to growing concerns over cyber risks facing the retail industry. Marks & Spencer Plc and the Co-op were targeted in a wave of attacks in 2025 that caused significant disruption, while Asos Plc said a breach of third-party communications platforms last month may have compromised customer data. Cyberattacks have also spilled into retailers’ physical infrastructure. Hackers targeted internet-connected refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets in October, while a second wave affected supermarkets across several other European countries.
